notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Isaiah 4, based on the trusted sources gathered. Where a tradition could not be found through the available searches, that is noted.

---

## v. 1 — The Desperation of the Daughters of Zion

**Traditional Reading (widely shared across traditions):**

The chapter division wrongly separates this verse from chapter 3; it is the climax of the judgment on the "daughters of Zion" described in Isaiah 3:16–26. After the slaughter of men in war (Isaiah 3:25), there will be such a scarcity of husbands that seven women (a number indicating many, not necessarily literal) will compete for one man. Desperate to escape the reproach of being unmarried and childless, they offer to forgo the normal legal provision of food and clothing that a husband owed his wives (Exodus 21:10) and will support themselves — asking only to bear his name and so remove their disgrace.

- **Ellicott**: "Those who had been wooed and courted, and had been proudly fastidious, should supplicate in eager rivalry (the seven women to one man implies a land depopulated by war, and so making polygamy natural) for the protection of marriage." The reproach is being childless — from the Jewish standpoint, "not only the great sorrow, but the great shame." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/4.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary**: "To take away" is actually the imperative "take thou away." Childlessness was a special reproach among Jews "because it took away all possibility of the woman being in the line of the Messiah's descent." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/4.htm
- **JFB (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown)**: The "seven" is an indefinite number; women "contrary to their natural bashfulness, would sue to one man to marry them." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/isaiah/4.htm
- **Enduring Word (Guzik, Pentecostal/Charismatic)**: Adds an application — in a broader sense, "it is not good for women to be too desperate for marriage. They may marry unwisely, and for the wrong reasons. It is also bad when women do not expect their husbands to provide for the household." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-4/
- **Gill (Baptist)**: Offers a spiritual application: the verse may be "accommodated in a spiritual sense to some professors of religion, who lay hold on Christ in a professional way, but spend their money for that which is not bread, and live upon their own duties and services, and not on Christ…" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-4.html

**Dispensational reading:** Some (e.g., Constable) see this as part of the future Tribulation judgment, when great numbers of men will perish, leaving women desperate. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-4.html

---

## v. 2 — The Branch of the LORD

**Traditional Reading:**

"In that day" shifts from judgment to Messianic hope. "The Branch of the LORD" (Hebrew *tsemach*) is universally recognised across Protestant traditions as a Messianic title for Jesus Christ. The same word is used in Jeremiah 23:5; 33:15; Zechariah 3:8; 6:12. The Branch is "beautiful and glorious" — for beauty and glory, i.e., for the ornament and glorification of Israel. "The fruit of the land" parallels "the Branch" and may also refer to Christ (as the grain of wheat, John 12:24) or to the restored fertility of the land under Messiah's reign. The beneficiaries are "the survivors of Israel" — the faithful remnant.

- **Ellicott**: This is "the first distinct prophecy in Isaiah of a personal Messiah." The interpretation that takes "the branch of the Lord" merely as "vegetation" misses the true meaning — "the acceptance of the term as Messianic by Jeremiah and Zechariah is surely conclusive." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/4.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary**: Both clauses are parallel: if the "Branch" is Messiah, so is "the fruit of the earth" — Christ is the grain of wheat that fell into the ground and died. The prophecy "was adequately fulfilled only in those who 'saved themselves' from the generation which rejected Christ. That remnant was the germ of the Catholic Church." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/4.htm
- **Gill (Baptist)**: The Branch is Messiah — "Christ is called 'the branch', not as God, but as man … it chiefly regards his descent from David, and when his family was very mean and low." He became "beautiful" being laden with the fruits of divine grace, and "glorious" through resurrection and exaltation. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-4.html
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: "The promise of the Messiah would be all the more beautiful and glorious to them in the midst of their suffering." The Branch carries "ideas of fruitfulness and life. Jesus used the same image when He said I am the vine, you are the branches (John 15:5)." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-4/
- **Geneva Study Bible (Reformed)**: Notes two interpretations — many take it as Messiah, but the Geneva note allows it may also mean "God's graces should be as plentiful toward the faithful as though they sprang out of the earth." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/isaiah-4.html
- **Precept Austin (Dispensational/Evangelical)**: "Isaiah 4:2-6 describes the future Messianic Age or Millennium and the Messiah's Reign … The Branch of the Lord (Jehovah) is the Lord Jesus Christ." The "survivors of Israel" are ethnic Jews who survive the Great Tribulation. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_42-6_commentary
- **Constable (Dispensational)**: Quotes the Scofield Reference Bible's fourfold use of "the Branch": (1) "the Branch of the LORD" (Immanuel character), (2) "the Branch of David" (kingly glory), (3) "the LORD's servant, the Branch" (humiliation), and (4) "the man whose name is THE BRANCH" (Son of man, Priest-King). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-4.html
- **Coffman (Churches of Christ)**: Insists the capital letter should be retained: "There is no reason to drop the capital letter and downgrade this reference to the fertility of the land." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/isaiah-4.html

---

## v. 3 — The Holy Remnant Recorded for Life

**Traditional Reading:**

The remnant left in Zion after judgment "will be called holy." This does not mean they earn holiness but that they are set apart by God. They are "everyone who is recorded among the living in Jerusalem" — a reference to the "book of life," the register of those destined for life in God's kingdom. The idea runs from Exodus 32:32 through to Revelation 21:27.

- **Ellicott**: The prophet envisions a new Jerusalem realising the ideal of Psalms 15 and 24, where everyone is called "holy" (cf. 1 Corinthians 1:2). The book of life "involves the idea of an election" but "excludes that of an irreversible predestination" — election must be "made sure" by a life in harmony with it (2 Peter 1:10). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/4.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary**: "Strikingly fulfilled in the fact that the early Christians were known as 'holy' or 'those called to be holy' in the first age (Acts 9:13, 32, 41; Romans 1:7, etc.)." But more — "the early Christians not only were called, but were holy." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/4.htm
- **Gill (Baptist)**: Holiness comes "through the imputation of the holiness of Christ unto them" and also through inherent grace implanted. Election is "the source and spring of holiness, and the security of the saints' final perseverance." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-4.html
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Holiness does not mean "super-spiritual" or "sinless perfection." It means "a life, a heart, a mind, and a body that is genuinely separated to the LORD … lived apart from the thinking and heart of this world, this flesh, and the devil." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-4/
- **Matthew Henry**: "Those only that are holy shall be left, when the Son of man shall gather out of his kingdom every thing which offends." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/isaiah/4.htm
- **Precept Austin**: The "recorded among the living" are those whose names are inscribed in the Lamb's book of life — "the only way to be holy is by grace through faith." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_42-6_commentary

**Reformed / Predestinarian reading:** Gill (Baptist, but strongly Calvinistic) emphasises that election is unconditional, personal, and the cause of holiness: "election is the source and spring of holiness." Ellicott (Anglican) balances this by noting that the book of life can have names blotted out (Revelation 3:5), so election is not irreversible.

---

## v. 4 — Cleansing by the Spirit of Judgment and Burning

**Traditional Reading:**

Holiness comes only after cleansing. The Lord washes away "the filth of the daughters of Zion" (the moral uncleanness described in Isaiah 3:16–24) and purges "the bloodstains" (blood-guiltiness from murder, oppression, and possibly child sacrifice to Molech). The instruments are "a spirit of judgment and a spirit of fire" — a purifying, refining process.

- **Ellicott**: "Spirit" is better taken literally as "breath or blast" (as in Isaiah 30:27–28; 40:7). The "blood" represents a greater enormity than the "filth" — one may be washed, but the other needs "the 'fiery baptism' of the wrath of Jehovah." The word for "burning" elsewhere means destruction generally (Deuteronomy 13:5; 17:7). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/4.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary**: "Sin must not be merely repented of and pardoned; it must be put away." The "blood of Jerusalem" may include child sacrifice — Ahaz and Manasseh "burnt [their] children in the fire," and the practice was widespread. "By a blast of burning; i.e., a fiery blast which shall destroy everything." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/4.htm
- **Gill (Baptist)**: Interprets "spirit of judgment" as a judicious spirit given to churches and ministers to discern and remove false doctrine, and "spirit of burning" as "a burning flaming zeal … against all false doctrine and worship." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-4.html
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: "The cleansing will not come easily; it will come by the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning. But it will be worth it." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-4/
- **Matthew Henry**: "By the judgment of God's providence, sinners were destroyed and consumed; but by the Spirit of grace they are reformed and converted. The Spirit herein acts as a Spirit of judgment, enlightening the mind, convincing the conscience; also as a Spirit of burning, quickening and strengthening the affections." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/isaiah/4.htm
- **Precept Austin**: The cleansing is a sovereign work of the Lord, paralleled in Zechariah 13:1: "In that day a fountain will be opened for the house of David … for sin and for impurity." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_42-6_commentary
- **Constable**: "The 'spirit' in view is probably the abstract concept of 'process' … A less probable view is that the spirit is the Holy Spirit." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-4.html
- **Geneva Study Bible**: The "blood" refers to "cruelty, extortion, malice and all wickedness." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/isaiah-4.html

---

## v. 5 — God's Re-Created Presence: Cloud and Fire

**Traditional Reading:**

The LORD will "create" — the verb is *bara* (as in Genesis 1:1), indicating a new, divine, creative act. Over Mount Zion and its assemblies, God will provide a cloud of smoke by day and flaming fire by night, echoing the Exodus pillar of cloud and fire (Exodus 13:21–22). This signals the tangible, manifest presence of God with His people. "Over all the glory there will be a canopy" — the Hebrew word for "canopy" (*chuppah*) is the same used for a marriage canopy, suggesting a bridal chamber over the glorified Zion.

- **Ellicott**: The word for "dwelling-place" (*makon*) is "almost invariably used for the tabernacle or temple." This determines that "assemblies" are "solemn assemblies" for worship, not political gatherings. "Upon all the glory shall be a defence" — the word occurs in Psalm 19:5 and Joel 2:16 and "is still used by Jews of the 'canopy' held over bride and bridegroom at a wedding." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/4.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary**: *Makon* seems "never to be used for anything but 'God's dwelling-place.'" The presence "shall rest like a canopy, protecting it." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/4.htm
- **Gill (Baptist)**: The cloud and fire signify "the presence of God with his churches in the latter day" — manifest, remarkable, protective, refreshing, and illuminating. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-4.html
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: "Just as in the days of the Exodus, God will be as real as a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-4/
- **Precept Austin**: This is "Jehovah's visible glory revealed" during the Millennium, a new Exodus-like manifestation. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_42-6_commentary
- **Geneva Study Bible**: "The faithful are called the glory of God because his image and tokens of his grace shine in them." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/isaiah-4.html

**The marriage imagery:** Ellicott's observation that *chuppah* is the Jewish wedding canopy is a distinctive note. Constable picks this up: "The daughters of Jerusalem tried desperately to secure husbands (Isaiah 4:1), but God Himself would finally provide a marriage canopy (chamber) for His beloved in the future." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-4.html

---

## v. 6 — A Shelter, Refuge, and Hiding Place

**Traditional Reading:**

The canopy becomes a "tabernacle" or booth (*sukkah*) — a shelter from desert heat by day and from storm and rain. The imagery is of complete protection. God Himself is the tabernacle, the refuge, the hiding place. The verse echoes Psalm 27:5 and 31:20.

- **Ellicott**: "In the manifested glory of Jehovah men would find, as the traveller finds in his tent, a protection against all forms of danger, against the scorching heat of noon, and against the pelting storm." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/4.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary**: "And it (i.e. 'the canopy') shall be a tabernacle, or bower, a shelter from the sun's heat by day, and from storm and rain both by day and night." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/4.htm
- **Gill (Baptist)**: Christ Himself is the tabernacle — "Christ, who tabernacled in our nature … will be spiritually present in the word and ordinances." The protection is "from the heat of a fiery law, which works wrath; from the flaming sword of justice … from Satan's temptations, compared to fiery darts; and from the violence of persecution." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-4.html
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: "Many people only want the LORD's constant presence and protection. But He doesn't grant those apart from His cleansing." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-4/
- **Matthew Henry**: "Only those who are weary will seek rest; only those who are convinced that a storm is approaching, will look for shelter." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/isaiah/4.htm

---

## Traditions: Where They Differ

**Dispensational vs. Amillennial / Historic Fulfilment:**

The main divide among Protestant traditions is over the timing of Isaiah 4:2–6:

- **Dispensational / Premillennial** (Precept Austin, Constable, earlier Scofield): Isaiah 4:2–6 describes the future Millennial reign of Christ on earth following the Great Tribulation. The "survivors of Israel" are ethnic Jews who survive the Tribulation and enter the Kingdom. The cloud and fire are literal manifestations of God's glory over restored Zion. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_42-6_commentary and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-4.html
- **Amillennial / Historic Fulfilment** (Pulpit Commentary, some Reformed): The prophecy was fulfilled spiritually in the early Church — the "escaped of Israel" are those who believed in Christ and escaped the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70. The "remnant was the germ of the Catholic Church." The cloud and fire are symbols of God's spiritual presence with the Church. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/4.htm
- **Gill (Baptist/postmillennial leaning)**: Sees the prophecy as referring to the latter-day glory of the Gospel church — a future golden age of the Church on earth before Christ returns, when false doctrine will be purged and God's presence will be manifest among the churches. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-4.html
- **Neither extreme** (Guzik/Enduring Word): Guzik reads the passage as speaking of the Messianic community in general, without dogmatically fixing the timing. He applies it to believers' experience of cleansing, presence, and protection now through Christ. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-4/

**Interpretation of "spirit of judgment" and "spirit of burning" (v. 4):**

- **Matthew Henry** sees the Spirit here as the Holy Spirit acting in conversion: "a Spirit of judgment, enlightening the mind … a Spirit of burning, quickening … the affections." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/isaiah/4.htm
- **Ellicott** sees it as "breath or blast" — a destructive blast of divine wrath. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/4.htm
- **Constable** sees it as an abstract "process." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-4.html
- **Gill** sees it as a spiritual gift of discernment and zeal given to the latter-day church. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-4.html
